title: Your T cells train in an organ that peaks at puberty and then withers
body: T cells are named after the thymus, the organ behind your breastbone where they mature. Inside, young cells face a brutal exam: those whose receptors fail to react die, and so do those that react strongly to the body’s own antigens, a guard against self-attack. The thymus grows until puberty, when it weighs **20 to 50 grams**, but after the first year of life its output of T cells begins to fall. Fat and connective tissue fill it in; by old age it weighs 5 to 15 grams and can be hard to find, though some T cell production continues through adult life.

left.label: At puberty
left.text: 20 to 50 grams, its relative maximum size.

right.label: In old age
right.text: 5 to 15 grams, with fat and connective tissue filling much of the space. It may be difficult to detect.

slides.heading: The exam inside
items: Immature T cells arrive from the bone marrow and start making receptors
No reaction, or a weak one: the cell dies
Strong reaction to the body’s own antigens: the cell dies
The survivors leave as T cells ready to fight infection

events.text: Known to the ancient Greeks; Galen noted it changes size over a lifetime
Jacques Miller discovers its immune role. Until then it was dismissed as an evolutionary accident

slides.question: What happens to a new T cell that reacts strongly to the body’s own antigens?
options: It is sent to the spleen
slides.explanation: Thymocytes that react strongly to self antigens die by apoptosis. Only cells that react, but not against the body itself, survive and leave.

slides.clue: The orderly form of cell death that removes T cells that fail the thymus exam
slides.detail: From the Greek for ‘falling off’, as leaves fall from a tree. Both the non-reactors and the self-attackers die this way.
